subject: Cognitive Science
title: The McGurk Effect
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The McGurk Effect.

hook.text: Watch a video of someone saying 'ga' while the audio plays 'ba.' You'll hear 'da.' A sound that doesn't exist.

buildup.text: The McGurk effect shows that speech perception isn't just auditory—your brain fuses visual lip movements with sound.

discovery.text: Discovered accidentally in 1976, it proves that hearing and vision are combined before conscious awareness.

twist.text: Close your eyes and the illusion vanishes. Open them and it returns—even if you know the trick.

climax.text: This is why phone calls feel harder than video calls. Without lip-reading cues, your brain has less input to work with.

punchline.text: What you see changes what you hear.

quiz.question: What causes the McGurk effect?
options: The brain fuses visual and auditory speech cues

details.summary: The McGurk effect occurs when visual speech movements conflict with an audio syllable, and the brain produces a third, blended percept. Seeing a mouth say 'ga' while hearing 'ba' makes you perceive 'da.' This demonstrates that speech perception is fundamentally multisensory.
details.whyItMatters: The McGurk effect proves that what you hear is not determined by sound alone. Vision routinely modifies auditory perception, even when you know about the illusion.
takeaways: Visual lip movements change what you hear
Conflicting audio and visual inputs produce a blended percept
Speech perception is inherently multisensory, not just auditory

faq.question: Does the McGurk effect go away if you know about it?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Even when you know the audio is always 'ba,' seeing a different mouth movement still alters your perception. Closing your eyes eliminates the effect immediately. This demonstrates that the audiovisual integration happens at a level below conscious control.

faq.question: Does the McGurk effect work in all languages?
faq.answer: The strength varies by language and culture. Japanese speakers show a weaker effect, possibly because Japanese culture emphasizes listening over watching the speaker's face. Languages that rely more on lip-reading for disambiguation in noisy environments tend to produce stronger effects.
